A parable of a person walking on a narrow place: if that place is not elevated above the ground, he shall walk quickly and not stumble, and all the more so not fall - but if that place is elevated above the ground, he shall think in his heart that he shall fall to the ground, and from his fear of falling he shall come to actually do so - so too, if he suspects that his fellow hates him too, he too shall hate him more - and whoever entertains an evil thought in his heart shall see that thing he imagined appear to him as true, and it shall become established in his heart and come to action - and so most dreams are nothing but imaginings a person entertains in his heart while awake, which appear to him in a dream.

And we learn in the Midrash: "behold, Pharaoh's army that came out to help you shall return to its land, to Egypt" (Jeremiah 37:7) - why did Pharaoh's army return to Egypt and not come to help Israel? Because they hated them - when they came to the shore of the sea and entertained in their hearts their hatred of Israel, from the evil thought, hatred, and imagining, there appeared to them, on the shore of the sea, inflated wineskins floating on the surface of the water - immediately they turned back, thinking these were the bodies of their own fathers whom the Holy One, blessed be He, had drowned in the sea through Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, and they said, it would be a disgrace for us to help our enemies who drowned our fathers in the sea, after having afflicted them with several plagues - from here we learn that hatred leads to enmity and quarrel.

And we learn in the Sifrei: "if men struggle" (Deuteronomy 25:11) - no peace comes forth from struggling - and so it says (Genesis 13:7), "and there was strife between the herdsmen of Abram's cattle and the herdsmen of Lot's cattle" - what caused Lot to separate from Abraham the righteous? Say, strife. And so it says (Deuteronomy 19:17), "then the two men who have the dispute shall stand" - what caused him to be struck? Say, strife. I know only of two men - from where do we know [it applies also to] a mother and daughter, or a man and woman? Scripture says "together" [yachdav, implying any two].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:4-16: It is taught (see Avot DeRabbi Natan, Zuta, chapter 9): a house in which there is strife is destined to be destroyed, and the Sages say, strife in a city means bloodshed in the city. A synagogue in which there is strife is destined to be destroyed, and some say it is destined to be scattered. Two Torah scholars dwelling in one city, and likewise two courts, and there is strife between them, are destined to die. Abba Shaul says, strife between courts is the destruction of the world.

In three places the Holy One, blessed be He, was patient concerning idolatry, but was not patient concerning strife. One: in the days of the generation of Enosh, they began to worship idols, as it is said (Genesis 4:26), "then it was begun to call in the name of the LORD [interpreted as idolatry]" - and He did not exact punishment from them until the generation of the Flood, in which there was strife among them, and they would rob and extort one another - and He was not patient with them, as it is said (ibid. 6:13), "the end of all flesh has come before Me." Second: in the generation of the wilderness, when they made the calf, He forgave them; but when they came to strife, He was not patient with them, for everywhere you find "and they murmured" you find punishment there. And greater than all of these was the strife of Korach, and therefore the Name dealt with Korach and his congregation beyond the letter of the law. Rabbi Berachya said, come and see how severe strife is - for the court below does not punish [capitally] until one is thirteen years and one day old, and the court above until one is twenty - but here even nursing infants perished, as it is said (Numbers 16:29), "if these die the common death of all men," and so on. Third: when the tribes divided over Judah and Benjamin and there was no peace between them, punishment came upon both - when the Ten Tribes sinned, the tribe of Judah came and exacted punishment from them, as it is said (II Chronicles 13:19), "and Aviyah pursued Jeroboam and captured cities from him: Bethel and its villages... and Jeroboam did not retain strength again in the days of Aviyah, and the LORD struck him and he died" - and although Jeroboam worshipped idols and the Holy One, blessed be He, was patient with him, once he divided against the tribe of Judah he was punished.

Rabbi Meir says, strife is severe, for even strife that is for the settling of the world is not called "good" - and in all the account of Creation "good" is said, but in the division of the firmament between waters and waters, "good" is not written of it. And is this not an a fortiori argument? If strife for the settling of the world is not called "good," strife for the destruction of the world - all the more so.

Strife is severe, for it is equal to the generation of the Flood - it is said of Korach's congregation (Numbers 16:2), "leaders of the congregation, summoned to the assembly, men of renown," and it is said of the generation of the Flood (Genesis 6:4), "who were of old, men of renown." Strife is severe, for it brings danger to life, as it is said (ibid. 13:12), "and he pitched his tent as far as Sodom" - because he separated from Abraham, he was close to being destroyed like Sodom, had it not been for the merit of Abraham our father, peace be upon him, as it is said (ibid. 19:29), "and God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot," and so on. Strife is severe, for it brings about death, as it is said (Exodus 21:22), "and if men struggle," and it is written, "and if there is a fatal injury," and so on.

Rabbi Yitzchak says, three are called wicked: one who raises his hand against his fellow, one who hardens his face, and one who borrows and does not repay. "One who raises his hand" - from where? As it is said (Exodus 2:13), "and he said to the wicked one, why do you strike your fellow?" - it does not say "you struck," but "why do you strike," teaching that he had not yet struck. "One who hardens his face" - from where? As it is said (Proverbs 21:29), "a wicked man hardens his face." "And one who borrows and does not repay" - from where? As it is said (Psalms 37:21), "the wicked borrows and does not repay." From where do we know that it is forbidden for a person to strike his fellow? As it is said (Deuteronomy 25:3), "forty he shall be struck, he shall not exceed" - and is this not an a fortiori argument? If one liable for lashes, we are commanded not to strike him more than the lashes prescribed, all the more so a person striking his fellow. From where do we know that it is forbidden to provoke one another? As it is said (Deuteronomy 2:19), "and when you draw near opposite the children of Ammon, do not distress them," and so on - and is this not an a fortiori argument? If Ammon and Moab, of whom Scripture said (ibid. 23:7), "you shall not seek their peace or their welfare," it is nevertheless said, "do not distress them and do not provoke them" - Israel toward one another, all the more so.

Severe is hatred, which destroyed the Temple, as we learn in Gittin (55b): "because of Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, Jerusalem was destroyed," and so on; see there. And there, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said, come and see the power of shame - for the Holy One, blessed be He, assisted Bar Kamtza and destroyed His own House and burned His own Sanctuary.

And because of the sin of baseless hatred Jerusalem was destroyed, and this is hinted at in "how [Eicha] does the city sit alone" (Lamentations 1:1) - the acrostic is EIVAH [enmity]. And we learn in Yoma (9b), it is taught: in the Second Temple, when they were expert and occupied with Torah and acts of kindness, why was it destroyed? Because of the baseless hatred that was among them - to teach you that baseless hatred is equal to idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed. And they, of blessed memory, said there, "for the bed is too short to stretch out on" (Isaiah 28:20) - what is "to stretch out"? From there being two evils [companions] as one [an idiom meaning contradictory things cannot coexist, applied here to hatred among peers].

And most of the suffering that comes upon a person is because of the sin of baseless hatred, as we learn in the chapter "Bameh Madlikin" (Shabbat 32b): it is taught, Rabbi Nechemiah says, because of the sin of baseless hatred, strife comes into a person's household, his wife miscarries, and his sons and daughters die while young.

And we have learned in Avot DeRabbi Natan (see chapter 16, section 1): Rabbi Yehoshua says, an evil eye, the evil inclination, and hatred of creatures drive a person from this world and from the World to Come. For whoever hates his fellow, the Holy One, blessed be He, uproots him from the world - for so we find with the people of Sodom, who were uprooted only because they hated one another, as it is said (Genesis 13:13), "and the men of Sodom were evil," and so on - "evil" to one another, and "sinners" in forbidden relations, "to the LORD" in idolatry, "exceedingly" in bloodshed.

And we learn in the Mechilta: "when you see the donkey of your enemy" (Exodus 23:5) - if you subdue your inclination to make your enemy your friend, I promise you that you shall make your enemy your friend, for it is written (Proverbs 16:7), "when the LORD is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies be at peace with him." And the sage said, one enemy should be in your eyes like a thousand thousand thousand enemies, and a thousand thousand thousand friends should be in your eyes like one. And although baseless hatred is a great sin, a person is obligated to hate the wicked just as he is obligated to love the fellows who walk in the straight path, as it is said (Psalms 139:21), "do I not hate those who hate You, LORD?"

Another explanation: "when you see the donkey of your enemy" - and if the Torah said this of one who hates him, and so on - all the more so of one who does not hate him. And David, peace be upon him, called the enemy by four disgraceful terms: violence, baseless, false, empty. "Violence," as it is written (Psalms 25:19), "see my enemies, for they are many, and they hate me with violent hatred" - these are those who hate the judges who acquit the innocent and convict the guilty, in order to seek out violence [profit through corrupt rulings]. "False," as it is said (ibid. 38:20), "and my enemies are vigorous and strong, and those who hate me falsely are many" - "their deceit is falsehood" (ibid. 119:118) - these are those who hate the upright because they speak truth, while they [the haters] seek to speak falsehood, calling evil good and good evil. "Empty," as it is said (ibid. 25:3), "let the treacherous be ashamed, empty-handed" - these are those who hate Torah scholars, who say there is judgment and there is a Judge, as though it were fitting to say the world is empty [without justice]. "Baseless" - "and words of hatred surrounded me, and they fought me without cause [chinam]" (ibid. 109:3) - these are those who hate their fellows for no reason, as it is said (ibid. 59:5), "without iniquity they run and prepare themselves; awake to meet me, and see."

A person should always love his fellow creatures, and this mitzvah is a positive commandment, as it is said (Leviticus 19:18), "and you shall love your neighbor as yourself." A person is obligated to love his fellow and have compassion on his wealth, as we learn (Avot, chapter 2, mishnah 12): Rabbi Yosei says, let your fellow's money be as dear to you as your own - and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained: just as a person looks after his own money, so he should look after his fellow's money, and just as he does not spread a bad name about his own money, so he should not spread a bad name about his fellow's money. If he sees his fellow in a place of danger, he is obligated to save him with all his ability, and if he does not save him, Scripture considers it as though he had killed him, as it is said (Leviticus 19:16), "you shall not stand idly by your fellow's blood" - and they, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 73a), if you see your fellow drowning in a river, or robbers coming upon him, you are obligated to save him, as it is said, "you shall not stand," and so on, and it is written (Proverbs 24:11), "save those taken to death," and so on - and if you say, who sees me? Why should I endanger myself, my own soul is at peace? Therefore Scripture says (ibid. 24:12), "if you say, behold, we did not know this - does not He who weighs hearts understand? And He who guards your soul, does He not know?" - and if he saves him, it is as though he sustained an entire world.

And even if he is his enemy or one who hates him, he is obligated to save him, as it is said (Exodus 23:5), "when you see the donkey of your enemy." And whoever does so, the Holy One, blessed be He, is pleased with his deeds, as it is said (Proverbs 16:7), "when the LORD is pleased with a man's ways" - meaning, if he desires that the Holy One, blessed be He, be pleased with his way, let him himself repay good to his enemies. How so? If he sees the ox or donkey of his fellow crouching under its burden, he shall help raise it up with him - immediately his enemy shall remove hatred from his heart, and for this the Holy One, blessed be He, shall be pleased with his way. And it is taught, whoever has adversaries above [i.e., in heaven], as we learn (Avot, chapter 3, mishnah 10), "whoever is pleasing to people," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 4:42-5: Therefore a person must restrain himself from strife, for whoever restrains himself from strife is honored among people, as it is said (Proverbs 20:3), "it is honor for a man to cease from strife," and it is written (ibid. 12:26), "the righteous has an advantage over his fellow, but the way of the wicked leads them astray." Explanation: the righteous has an advantage over another person, in that the righteous hears his own disgrace and endures his desire and subdues his inclination and is silent, so as not to come to strife and disgrace - "but the way of the wicked leads them astray" - the evil way of the wicked leads them astray, since it is a disgrace in their eyes to hear their own disgrace and be silent, and they stray from the way of reason, so that through this they come to quarrel and murder. And we learn in Chullin (see 89a): Rabbi Ilai said, the world endures only through the merit of one who restrains his mouth at a time of quarrel, as we copied its words above in chapter 3. And the sage said, no person ever disgraced me more than once, for the first time I bear his disgrace, and he shall not disgrace me a second time.

And we learn in the Midrash: "a man of friends [may come] to ruin" (Proverbs 18:24) - whoever wishes to have friends must endure and overlook wrongs against himself, and receive them with a pleasant countenance. Explanation: "lehitro'e'a" [to have friends] is derived from "rei'a" [friend], meaning, he should make himself a friend and companion to every person. Another explanation of "a man of friends," and so on: a person shall never have friends unless he submits before them and breaks his own desire, derived from (Psalms 2:9), "you shall break them with an iron rod" - and then his companionship shall be fine and complete. And the sage said, whoever has not broken his pride before his fellow, and is not always the one insulted by them rather than the insulter of any of them, shall not have friends.

And these good attributes cause a person to have friends more beloved than his own brothers, as it is said (Proverbs 18:24), "but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother," and it is written (ibid. 27:10), "do not forsake your own friend or your father's friend" - if you keep and do not forsake your own friend or your father's friend, you shall not need your brother on the day of your calamity, for your friend shall save you on your day of trouble, being more to you than a brother.

And we learn in Shemot Rabbah (27:1): "better a close neighbor" - this is Jethro - "than a distant brother" - this is Esau. Of Jethro it is written (I Samuel 15:6), "and you showed kindness to all the children of Israel," and so on; of Esau it is written (Deuteronomy 25:17), "remember what Amalek did to you." You find many matters proving that they are written of Esau disparagingly and of Jethro praisingly. Of Esau it is written (Lamentations 5:11), "they afflicted the women in Zion"; of Jethro it is written (Exodus 2:21), "and he gave Zipporah his daughter to Moses." Of Esau it is written (Psalms 14:4), "who devour my people, they eat bread"; of Jethro it is written (Exodus 2:20), "call him, that he may eat bread." Of Esau it is written (Deuteronomy 25:18), "and did not fear God"; of Jethro it is written (Exodus 18:23), "and God shall command you." Esau abolished sacrifices; of Jethro it is written (Exodus 18:12), "and Jethro took a burnt offering and sacrifices," and so on. Esau heard of their going out and came to fight them, as it is said (Exodus 17:8), "and Amalek came" - while Jethro heard of their good fortune and came to join them, as it is said (Exodus 18:1), "and Jethro heard," and so on.

And righteous converts are equal to Israel in love, and are like Israel in all their matters, and it is a positive commandment to love the convert, as it is said (Deuteronomy 10:19), "and you shall love the convert." And we learn in the Mechilta: "and you shall not oppress a convert" (Exodus 22:20) - you shall not oppress him with words, and you shall not press him for money. "With words" - that you not say to him, yesterday you were worshipping idols, and pig's meat was still between your teeth, and now you stand and speak against me! And if you oppress him, he shall oppress you, as it is said, "for you were converts in the land of Egypt." From here Rabbi Natan used to say, do not tell your fellow of your own blemish [i.e. do not accuse another of a fault you share].

And we learn in Bava Metzia (59b): our Rabbis taught, whoever oppresses a convert transgresses three prohibitions, and whoever presses him [for money] transgresses two. It is taught, Rabbi Eliezer says, why did the Torah warn concerning the convert in thirty-six places? Because it is written, "for you were converts."

Beloved are converts, whom the Holy One, blessed be He, weighed equal to the holiness of the Sabbath and to holiness from idolatry - for Scripture warned concerning the Sabbath in twenty-eight places, and concerning idolatry in twenty-eight places, and concerning the convert too there is warning in twenty-eight places.

And Israel are called holy, as it is said (Deuteronomy 14:2), "for you are a holy people," through being sanctified from idolatry, as it is said (Leviticus 20:7), "and you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy" - from forbidden relations, from carcasses and torn animals, from detestable things and creeping things, from impurities. From forbidden relations, as it is said at the end of the section on forbidden relations, "and you shall sanctify yourselves." From carcasses and torn animals, as it is said (Exodus 22:30), "and you shall be men of holiness to Me." From detestable things and creeping things, as it is said at the end of the section on forbidden foods (Leviticus 11:44), "for I am the LORD your God, and you shall sanctify yourselves and be holy." From impurities, as it is said (ibid. 16:19), "and shall cleanse it and sanctify it from the impurities of the children of Israel." Even in the future to come, the Holy One, blessed be He, shall sanctify them, as it is said (Ezekiel 37:28), "and the nations shall know that I, the LORD, sanctify Israel" - and so it says, "you shall be holy to Me" in this world, "and I shall separate you from the peoples to be Mine" in the World to Come. Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus says, had it said, "and I shall separate the peoples from you," there would have been no possibility of restoration for the nations of the world, and there would have been no opening for any of them to convert - to what is this comparable? To one who sorts bad from good; he does not return to the bad ones, lest he find good among them [i.e. the wording preserves opportunity for conversion].

Beloved are converts, for in every place Scripture warns Israel [with a term], Israel is called by it, converts too are called by it. Israel are called servants, as it is said (Leviticus 25:55), "for the children of Israel are servants to Me," and converts are called servants, as it is said (Isaiah 56:6), "and the sons of the foreigner who join themselves to the LORD, to serve Him and to love the name of the LORD, to be His servants." Israel are called ministers, as it is said (ibid. 61:6), "but you shall be called the priests of the LORD; men shall call you the ministers of our God," and converts are called ministers, as it is said, "and the sons of the foreigner who join themselves to the LORD to serve Him." Israel are called beloved, as it is said (Malachi 1:2), "I have loved you, says the LORD," and converts are called beloved, as it is said (Deuteronomy 10:18), "and He loves the convert." Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says, "and those who love Him are like the sun going forth" (Judges 5:31) - whoever loves the Omnipresent, the Omnipresent loves him; of converts it is written, "and He loves the convert," and of the righteous it is written, "and those who love Him are like the sun going forth in its might." And who is greater - one who loves the king, or one whom the king loves? By way of parable, everyone loves their own king, but happy is he whose king loves him.

Onkelos the convert asked Rabbi Eliezer, is this the entirety of the affection with which the Holy One, blessed be He, cherished the convert, to give him only bread and clothing (Deuteronomy 10:18)? He said to him, and is that a small thing in your eyes - a thing that that elder [Jacob] pleaded for, saying (Genesis 28:20), "and give me bread to eat," and so on? He came before Rabbi Yehoshua, who began to appease him, saying to him, "bread" here is the bread of Torah, as it is said (Proverbs 9:5), "come, eat of my bread," and "clothing" is Torah, as it is said (Isaiah 3:6), "clothing, be our leader." And moreover, their [the converts'] daughters marry into the priesthood and bear priests, and they merit "bread and clothing" - "bread" is the showbread, and "clothing" is the priestly garments - this is within the Sanctuary; and from where also outside its bounds? "Bread" is the challah [dough-offering], and "clothing" is the first shearing.

Of Israel "covenant" is said, as it is said (Genesis 17:13), "and My covenant shall be in your flesh," and of converts "covenant" is said, as it is said (Isaiah 56:4), "and hold fast to My covenant." Of Israel "favor" [ratzon] is said, as it is said (Exodus 28:38), "for favor for them before the LORD," and of converts "favor" is said, as it is said (Isaiah 56:7), "their burnt offerings and their sacrifices shall be favorably [accepted] on My altar." Of Israel "guarding" is said, as it is said (Psalms 121:3), "behold, He who guards Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps," and of converts "guarding" is said, as it is said (ibid. 146:9), "the LORD guards the converts." And so you find converts among the four groups who answer and say before Him who spoke and the world came into being (cf. Isaiah 44:5): this one shall say, I am the LORD's - these are Israel. And this one shall call himself by the name of Jacob - these are righteous converts. And this one shall write with his hand, "to the LORD" - these are penitents. And [this one] shall be surnamed by the name of Israel - these are those who fear Heaven.

Rabbi says, a convert who comes to convert is as though he had done a kindness to all of Israel - for so Saul said to the sons of Jethro (I Samuel 15:6), "and you showed kindness to all the children of Israel" - and is there anyone who could do a kindness to all those thousands and myriads? Rather, since he converted among them, [it is as though everyone] said (Exodus 18:10), "blessed is the LORD who saved you" - as though he had done a kindness to all of them.
